en: The Fifty Verses on the Method of Serving the Teacher, compiled by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master from the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of Xuanfan, and Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Rìchēng.
Based upon the various sūtras, vinayas, and secret teachings, I have briefly set forth this ritual manual for serving the master.
Having heard it, those who rejoice and give rise to a pure mind shall attain the vajra-wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If one prostrates and pays homage to the consecrated master at the three times of day,
one has thereby made offerings to all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Arising with the highest reverence, one joins the palms while holding flowers.
Having dispersed that maṇḍala, one should prostrate with the crown of the head at his feet.
Whether that teacher is a layperson or one who has newly received full ordination,
by placing scriptures and images before him, all doubts and slanders will cease.
If a disciple who has left the household life constantly serves with a pure mind,
rising when the teacher has sat down and greeting them upon arrival— provided only that the formal prostration is omitted—
the teacher and the disciple should both examine each other's capacity.
If one does not first investigate, both will incur an offense against the Dharma.
If one is full of anger and lacks compassion, or is greedy, distracted, arrogant,
and relies on one's lineage, one should exercise discernment when bestowing gifts.
Possessing the precepts, patience, compassion, and wisdom; Reverent and free from deceit;
Thoroughly understanding the secret ritual protocols; Extensively familiar with all treatises;
Skilled in the characteristics of mantras and The activities of the maṇḍala.
Having realized the ten true suchnesses, all their faculties are completely purified.
If those who seek the Dharma treat the teacher with contempt or disparagement,
they slander all the Tathāgatas and will constantly experience various sufferings and afflictions.
Due to excessive delusion, one reaps immediate retribution;
seized by malevolent planets, bound by the afflictions of grave illness,
oppressed by royal law, and bitten by venomous snakes.
From the perils of enemies, thieves, water, and fire, and when non-humans find their opportunity,
those Piśācas constantly create all manner of obstacles;
having met their end from this, they shall immediately fall into the evil realms.
Do not cause even the slightest affliction to arise in the Ācārya;
through ignorance and opposition, he will certainly enter the Avīci Hell and undergo various extreme sufferings— of this, it is said, one should be deeply afraid.
Because one slanders the ācārya and constantly dwells within that [state of mind],
and because that ācārya extensively upholds the treasury of the True Dharma,
one should therefore be single-minded and never give rise to contempt or disparagement.
By constantly serving and making offerings to the ācārya,
and by generating a heart of reverence, one will eliminate obstacles and afflictions.
Furthermore, in the presence of the teacher, one should joyfully practice generosity.
He did not seek even for his own body, let alone for material wealth;
having practiced with courageous diligence throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas,
he has now finally realized Bodhi— this is truly most rare.
Guard well your profound vows, make offerings to all Tathāgatas,
and revere your ācāryas as equal to all Buddhas.
Even if it be the most excellent of all precious objects you possess, [you should offer them].
Seeking inexhaustible bodhi, I offer this with a sincere heart.
By bestowing upon the Buddha and the ācārya, my merit increases in every thought-moment;
this is the most supreme field of merit, through which one swiftly attains the fruit of bodhi.
One who seeks the Dharma in this way, possessing the virtues of precepts and patience,
and not deceiving the teacher, shall attain vajra-wisdom.
If one steps upon the teacher’s shadow with their feet, they incur a sin equal to that of destroying a stupa.
Regarding bedding, seats, and requisites, the transgression of riding over them is a fault.
If the teacher gives instruction, one should listen with joy;
if one is personally unable to comply, then one should respectfully explain the reason with kind words.
Because one relies upon the teacher, all undertakings are accomplished;
for the sake of present happiness and rebirth in heaven, how could one dare to disobey his command?
One should protect the teacher’s wealth and property as if they were one's own life.
One should attend upon those [teachers] as if they were one's own kin, always serving them with respect.
One should not, in the presence of the teacher, cover one’s head,
ride in a carriage, stand on tiptoe, place hands on the hips, or sit or lie down at ease.
If circumstances require one to sit, do not extend both legs;
always maintain all dignified deportment, and if the teacher rises, you should rise immediately.
When at the place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), you should not follow behind as they take their steps.
Stand with dignity and composure at one’s side; do not discard mucus or saliva.
Nor should one speak privately before the teacher, nor engage in whispering, laughter, singing, dancing, or chanting in his presence.
Whether he orders one to sit or to rise, one should each respond with calm and respectful decorum;
if on a dangerous path, having informed him, one should act as a guide.
Furthermore, one should not manifest signs of physical fatigue before him.
When snapping the fingers of the knuckles, leaning against a pillar or a wall,
washing clothes or feet, bathing, or performing similar tasks,
one must first inform the teacher so that he may be aware; one must not perform such actions while being seen by him.
Furthermore, one should never casually utter the name of one's teacher;
even if someone should insistently ask, one should show them but a single character.
If the teacher should command one to perform a task, one should wait for him to dispatch a messenger.
Regarding the tasks to be performed there, one should maintain mindfulness and never forget them.
Whether laughing, spitting, stretching, or yawning, one should cover the mouth with the hand;
if there is a matter to report, one should do so with a bowed body and gentle speech.
If a woman living at home comes with a pure mind to hear the Dharma,
joining her palms and maintaining dignified deportment, gazing intently upon the face of the teacher;
having heard it, she should uphold it and abandon all pride.
Always as if newly married, she lowers her face in modesty and shame.
Regarding those ornaments for adorning the body, she no longer feels attachment or delight;
since they do not correspond with what is wholesome, she contemplates them all with a desire to distance herself from them.
One should always admire the teacher’s virtue and not look for minor faults;
by following their instructions, one attains accomplishment, whereas seeking out faults will surely lead to one's own ruin.
Through teaching the Dharma, one delivers disciples; through the maṇḍala and homa rites, one brings them to fruition.
When residing with the same teacher in a city or town, one should not perform any action without his instruction.
Whatever is obtained through preaching the Dharma, or whatever pure offerings of wealth and goods are received, all should be presented to the teacher; he may then use them as he sees fit.
Fellow students and dharma heirs should not act as disciples,
nor should they receive the rites of service and veneration from their teacher.
If one offers an object to the teacher, one should hold it with both hands and present it.
If the teacher has anything to bestow, always receive it with reverence upon the crown of your head.
Devote yourself exclusively to practicing right conduct, always remembering and upholding it without forgetfulness.
If others act contrary to the discipline, instruct them with words of loving-kindness.
If, due to illness or other causes, one is unable to carry out what the teacher has instructed, one should perform a prostration and explain the situation; thus, there will be no fault.
One should always cause the teacher to rejoice and remain free from all afflictions.
One should practice this with diligence; fearing prolixity, I have not described it further.
That Vajra Tathāgata personally proclaimed this, as well as what is clarified in other teachings:
by relying on the master, one attains accomplishment.
If a disciple is pure and can take refuge in the Triple Gem,
even if their life is about to end, one should still proclaim the essentials of the Dharma and transmit the secret teachings,
enabling them to become a true vessel for the Dharma.
If one recites and maintains [this] while manifesting signs, one shall incur a root offense.
If one can follow and train according to the teacher’s practice, then all merits will be accomplished.
By means of these roots of goodness gathered by me, may I and all sentient beings swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Fifty Verses on the Method of Serving the Teacher (Śiṣyalekha)
